title: Visualisers: The Classroom Tool I Can't Teach Without
author: Anna Sutton
summary: Anna Sutton, deputy head and primary teacher-trainer at The Educakers, argues that the humble document-camera visualiser is one of the two classroom tools she could never teach without, alongside mini-whiteboards. She contends that visualisers reduce cognitive load by making the 'where do I write this, how should it look' questions disappear, since pupils can see the exact expected output built up step by step under the camera rather than reconstructed from a teacher's verbal instructions. Drawing on Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction and Dylan Wiliam's claim that cognitive load theory is the single most important idea for teachers to know, she frames visualiser use as a practical enactment of modelling: breaking down thinking into small, visible steps rather than presenting only a finished answer. She contrasts two classroom scenarios — modelling on a flip chart versus modelling live under a visualiser — to show how the latter produces neater, more organised pupil work and faster live marking. The piece closes with a five-item starter checklist for getting a visualiser lesson-ready and a challenge to try it in tomorrow's lesson.
points: Visualisers reduce cognitive load by removing ambiguity about 'where do I write this, how should it look' so pupils can copy an actual modelled layout rather than reconstruct instructions from memory.
Sutton frames visualiser modelling as a direct, low-effort way to enact Rosenshine's principle of breaking new material into small steps and providing models.
A side-by-side comparison of flip-chart modelling versus visualiser modelling shows the visualiser version produces measurably neater, more organised pupil work and faster live marking.
Visualisers aren't just for teacher modelling — letting pupils place their own books under the camera turns editing and celebrating success into a whole-class, real-time activity.
The EEF's point that digital tools strengthen feedback by making pupil work visible gives the practice an evidence-based backing beyond Sutton's own classroom experience.
quotes: I've even been in classrooms where the visualiser is plugged in but abandoned on the floor, buried under books. Not because teachers don't want to use it—because no one has shown them how. And that's not their fault.
Visualisers help us manage that load. They take unnecessary thinking away — Where do I write this? How should it look? Which bit goes here? — so pupils can focus on the actual learning.
You model a written addition on a big piece of flip chart paper. You remind them: neat layout, one digit per box, line up the digits. They start work.
You model the calculation under your visualiser using your own teacher model book. You show one digit per box, lay out the next calculation underneath, explain your thinking aloud. They start work.
Now you can live mark effectively. You can see misconceptions easily. Children can self-check. You're not repeating yourself.

Children can share their writing by placing their book under the visualiser. Their classmates can follow the text, celebrate success, and support editing. This kind of modelling is powerful because the class can see real writing, in a real book, in real time.
